text: Ask three teams for last quarter's revenue and you can get three different numbers. Nobody is lying. Each team wrote its own logic against the same tables. A semantic layer exists to stop that. This chapter is conceptual: first the idea, then how Salesforce builds it.

Same table, three answers. Sales counts closed won amounts. Finance subtracts refunds. Marketing includes deals still open. A table has columns, but it does not say which stages count, which date defines this quarter, or what gets netted out. That knowledge lives in analysts' heads.

A semantic layer sits between your data and everything that consumes it. Define the business logic once, in one governed place, and dashboards, analysis, and AI assistants all reuse it. You already know a small version: a T-SQL view. This is the same instinct across the whole stack.

In Salesforce, the semantic layer is the semantic model, powered by Tableau Semantics. This is the real Semantic Layer area, with a list of models and a Metrics tab. Note the older Data Cloud name in the screenshot. The product is now called Data 360, but the concept is unchanged.

Open a model in the builder and you see the parts. Data objects, joined by relationships, with calculated fields and metrics layered on top. The objects can be data model objects, data lake objects, or calculated insights. Good semantics also give AI assistants the business context they need to answer consistently.
A semantic layer turns raw tables into shared business meaning, so disagreements about the number get settled once, in one place. Next up: defining metrics and KPIs centrally.
